findings.title: Canonicalize email addresses before matching blocked entries
findings.body: Blocked emails are stored as ordinary strings and matched with case-sensitive equality, without normalization. A block for `bad@SpamClub.com` therefore does not match `bad@spamclub.com`, although email domains are case-insensitive and these identify the same mailbox. Mixed-case block imports or differently cased input can silently bypass the block. Normalize stored addresses and lookup values consistently using the application's email canonicalization.

findings.title: An empty email error array incorrectly rejects a valid address
findings.body: The new EmailValidator reads `record.errors[:email]` even when the email is valid, which creates an empty array entry in ActiveModel::Errors. If registration fails for another field, such as a username taken after the availability check, `errors.to_hash` can return `email: []`. Empty arrays are truthy in JavaScript, so this condition caches the valid email as rejected and disables resubmission even after the username is corrected. Require a nonempty email error array before rejecting the address.

findings.title: Rejected user saves roll back the block-match statistics
findings.body: When email validation runs inside `User#save` or `save!`, this nested save participates in the user's transaction. Adding the blocked-email validation error causes the outer save to fail and roll back both the counter increment and `last_match_at`. For example, `User.create_for_email` calls `save!` without a preceding standalone validation, so its rejected attempts leave no match statistics. The direct `should_block?` tests do not exercise this rollback. Record attempt statistics outside the transaction that rejects the user.

findings.title: Update match counters atomically
findings.body: The counter is updated through an unlocked read-modify-save sequence. Two concurrent checks for the same address can both read a count of N and save N+1, losing one match; out-of-order saves can also replace `last_match_at` with an older timestamp. This makes the blocking statistics unreliable under concurrent requests. Use an atomic database increment and a concurrency-safe timestamp update, or lock the row.
